summary: This document defines how to signal Entropy Label Capability and Entropy Readable Label Depth using OSPFv2, OSPFv3 and BGP-LS. These let an ingress router know whether it can insert entropy labels for load-balancing into an MPLS path.

eli5.summary: Routers need to tell each other that they understand special random tags used to share traffic over roads. This document tells them how to say so in OSPF.

questions: what is entropy readable label depth
subtitle: How OSPF routers tell each other whether they can handle entropy labels and how deep they can read a label stack.

tldr.problem: An ingress router cannot insert entropy labels for load-balancing unless the egress has signaled it can process them, and it also benefits from knowing how deep each router can read the label stack.
tldr.mechanism: A new E-Flag in OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 prefix advertisements signals Entropy Label Capability, and the ERLD is carried in the Node MSD TLV; BGP-LS can carry both onward.
tldr.outcome: Ingress routers can learn these capabilities from OSPF or BGP-LS and decide whether and where to insert entropy labels.

facts.label: OSPFv2 E-Flag
facts.value: 0x20 in the Extended Prefix TLV Flags

today: RFC 9089 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2021. No RFC obsoleting or updating it is recorded.

sections.title: Why Signal ELC and ERLD
sections.content:
RFC 6790 describes using Entropy Labels (EL) to load-balance MPLS traffic flows. It introduces the Entropy Label Capability (ELC) and defines signaling of it through MPLS signaling protocols. This document adds signaling of the ELC using OSPFv2 and OSPFv3.

With Segment Routing over the MPLS data plane, ingress routers also benefit from knowing each intermediate router's Entropy Readable Label Depth (ERLD), defined in RFC 8662. It helps the ingress decide where to put the EL in the stack and whether several ELs are needed at different positions.
sections.eli5: Routers split traffic over many roads using a random-looking tag. Before adding a tag, the sender wants to know who can read it and how far down the pile of labels they can look.

sections.title: Advertising ELC in OSPF
sections.content:
ELC is a property of a node, but the RFC says it is useful to attach it to a prefix. In multi-area or multi-domain networks, a router may not know who originated a remote prefix or what that originator can do.

A router with several interfaces MUST NOT announce ELC unless all of its interfaces can process ELs. If they all can, it SHOULD advertise the ELC with every local host prefix it advertises in OSPF.
sections.eli5: A router only says it understands the tags if every one of its doors does. Then it puts the note on every address it announces.

sections.title: ELC in OSPFv2 and OSPFv3
sections.content:
In OSPFv2, the Extended Prefix TLV from RFC 7684 has a one-octet Flags field. The new E-Flag is 0x20, set by the advertising router to show the prefix originator can process ELs. An ABR MUST preserve it by originating an Extended Prefix Opaque LSA with the received ELC setting. An ASBR redistributing a prefix SHOULD preserve it the same way, with the flooding scope matching the LSA it originates for the redistribution.

In OSPFv3, the E-Flag is bit 0x40 in the PrefixOptions field of RFC 5340. An ABR MUST set it in the Inter-Area-Prefix-LSA or Inter-Area-Prefix TLV to the value in the source area. An ASBR SHOULD preserve the value in the AS-External-LSA, NSSA-LSA or External-Prefix TLV. How ELC is exchanged between protocol instances on an ASBR is out of scope.
sections.eli5: There is a tiny checkbox on each address announcement. Border routers must copy the checkbox when they pass the announcement along.

sections.title: Advertising ERLD in OSPF
sections.content:
The ERLD is carried in a Node Maximum SID Depth (MSD) TLV from RFC 8476, using the ERLD-MSD type defined in RFC 9088.

If a router's interfaces differ in how deep they can read the label stack, it MUST advertise the smallest value across all interfaces. Missing ERLD-MSD advertisements only mean the node does not support advertising the capability. If the ERLD-MSD type shows up in an OSPFv2 or OSPFv3 Link MSD sub-TLV, it MUST be ignored.
sections.eli5: If a router has doors that can look at different depths, it reports the shallowest one, so nobody expects too much.

sections.title: Carrying the Data in BGP-LS
sections.content: The OSPF extensions can be distributed through BGP-LS (RFC 7752) using existing TLVs. ELC is advertised in the Prefix Attribute Flags TLV from RFC 9085, and ERLD-MSD in the Node MSD TLV from RFC 8814.
sections.eli5: The same notes can be copied onto a larger bulletin board that outside systems read, using forms that already exist.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document advertises extra node capabilities, so the security considerations of RFC 5340, RFC 7684, RFC 7752, RFC 7770, RFC 8476, RFC 8662, RFC 8814 and RFC 9085 apply.

Wrongly setting the E-Flag while originating, propagating or redistributing may lead to poor or no load-balancing, or to MPLS traffic being discarded on the egress node. A wrong ERLD value may lead to poor or no load-balancing.
sections.eli5: If a router says the wrong thing about the tags, traffic may be shared badly or even thrown away.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA allocated flag 0x20 in the "OSPFv2 Extended Prefix TLV Flags" registry and bit 0x40 in the "OSPFv3 Prefix Options (8 bits)" registry, both as the E-Flag (ELC Flag).
sections.eli5: The two new checkboxes were given official spots so they do not clash with others.
